title: Nahusha's question: who is a brahmin?
hookLine: a giant serpent, a trapped brother, and the question: who is a brahmin?
carry: varna by birth or by conduct? hear both
tomorrow: is a kind lie ever better than a hard truth?

cards: In a mountain forest, Bhima, the strongest of the Pandava brothers, is caught in the coils of a giant serpent, and for once he can't break free. His brother Yudhishthira finds him.
The serpent says: answer my questions, and I'll let him go. The first question is one Hindus still argue about: who is a brahmin?

teach.b: Yudhishthira answers: the one in whom you see truth, generosity, forgiveness, good conduct, gentleness, self-discipline and compassion. The serpent pushes back: those are found in a shudra too.

Then, says Yudhishthira, a shudra with those marks is not a shudra, and a brahmin without them is not a brahmin. The serpent turns out to be King Nahusha, cursed long ago; the answers free him, and Bhima with him.
Varna is the word for the four classes: brahmins, priests and teachers; kshatriyas, rulers and warriors; vaishyas, traders and farmers; shudras, who serve.
Yudhishthira's answer is the conduct side, and it has lines in Manu too: a twice-born man who neglects the Veda sinks, while still alive, to a shudra's state, and rank can rise and fall.
In the Gita, Krishna says the four were made by qualities and action. Reformers like Dayananda Saraswati read varna this way. The birth side has its best case.
Manu's first chapter has the four come from the creator's mouth, arms, thighs and feet, a picture from a Rig Veda hymn, and its rules on marriage, duty and punishment follow birth.
Traditional commentators read it so, and read the rising and falling as change over generations, not in one life. Two readings, each with verses.

teach.h: GIVE THE OTHER SIDE ITS BEST CASE.
teach.b: Before choosing, give the other side its best case.

how: Hindu teachers and reform movements have long debated how to read varna; in study circles, Yudhishthira's answer to the serpent Nahusha and Gita 4.13 on qualities and action are often read beside the Manusmriti's verses on birth (1.31).

p: the serpent who asks who is a brahmin
the four from the creator's body
a brahmin can fall by how he lives

s: the Manusmriti never hints that varna can change
it says a twice-born who neglects the Veda sinks to a shudra's state, and that rank can rise and fall.
in the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira tells the serpent a brahmin is known by conduct
truth, generosity, forgiveness, compassion; without them, he says, a brahmin is not a brahmin.
Manu's picture of the four from the creator's body echoes a Rig Veda hymn
the hymn of the cosmic person has the same picture: mouth, arms, thighs, feet.

games.q: your seminar assigns you to argue that, in Manu, varna is by birth. you disagree. what's your strongest honest opening?
o: chapter one makes the four from the creator's body, and its rules follow birth.
Manu never mentions varna; later readers added it.
Krishna says in the Gita that varna comes from qualities and action.
games.why: that's the birth side's best case, from the text itself. the Gita line belongs to the other side; a good debater knows both.

practice: Sit toward one side of your chair and, silently, give one reason for the view you hold. Then shift your weight to the other side and give the other view its best reason, as if it were yours.
Settle in the middle, and breathe there until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The Manusmriti: a book whose varna rules follow birth, with verses that both sides of the debate still point to, as Yudhishthira did.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the word Manu uses for the four classes.

carryVoice: For the road: varna, by birth or by conduct? Yudhishthira answered the serpent; you give the other side its best case first. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana (Aranyaka) Parva, the Ajagara episode (Bhima seized by the serpent Nahusha; Yudhishthira answers who is a brahmin: truth, generosity, forgiveness, good conduct, gentleness, austerity, compassion)
Manusmriti 1.31 and 1.87–1.91 (the four from the creator's mouth, arms, thighs and feet; their duties)
Rig Veda 10.90.12 (the Purusha hymn: the same picture)
Manusmriti 2.168 (a twice-born who neglects the Veda sinks, while living, to a shudra's state) and 10.64–10.65 (a shudra may attain a brahmin's rank and a brahmin sink to a shudra's)
Bhagavad Gita 4.13 (the four made according to qualities and action)
